rationale: Against 2,416 blinded human labels raw Jev was miscalibrated (slope 1.63, Spiegelhalter test rejected, mean probability 4.8% vs weighted base rate 2.7%: under-extreme and level-shifted, not over-confident); of two frontier arms one was worse (slope 2.55) and one better (ECE 0.0027 vs 0.0231); out-of-fold Platt recalibration cut pooled ECE 0.0231 to 0.0069 (Sec. 4.2, 4.4, Table 9).

Coded 195,857 Texas crash narratives at about $0.154 per 1,000 vs $7.95 for a mid-tier LLM (52x), with F1 0.908 vs 0.967 and 0.885 for two frontier models against human labels; probabilities usable for ranking but prevalence counts need per-variable recalibration and a review budget over flagged records (Sec. 4.1, 4.3-4.4, 5).

On 15 preregistered CSS annotation tasks (7,977 items) Jev trails the per-task best LLM on 14 of 15 with a median deficit of 11.6 macro-F1 points, significant after FDR correction on 12; the 0.6B open RLCD model is far lower (median macro-F1 0.361 vs 0.581) (Sec. 4.1, Table 1).

Preregistered hypothesis that calibration degrades on Indian English dialect text was rejected in the opposite direction: Jev's dialect ECE 0.063 was the lowest of 22 models (next 0.181) and its F1 the only positive point estimate vs the best LLM (+4.2, CI -3.9 to +11.5); a single dialect task, which the authors say cannot certify fairness (Sec. 4.3).

Median ECE 0.157 [0.108, 0.233] beat the verbalised confidence of 16 of 19 LLMs but not three frontier Claude models (0.066-0.075; intervals overlap); on empathy 78% of items had confidence >=0.9 at accuracy 0.383 (ECE 0.538), and the preregistered calibration hypothesis was unsupported (Sec. 4.2, 4.4).

Preregistered confidence cascades matched or beat the partner LLM at lower cost (Gemini 0.674 vs 0.678 at 56% cost; Gemma 0.638 vs 0.626; Haiku 0.639 vs 0.622 at 27% cost), but the preregistered routing hypothesis (>=0.85 accuracy at confidence >=0.9 with >=15% coverage) failed, clearing only 6 of 14 tasks (Sec. 4.4-4.5).

With arithmetic in code and semantic relations asked as atomic Choices, Jev got 100/100 semantic and 50/50 downstream-exact answers, tied with five other configurations; the seven wrong intermediate selections that correct final labels concealed (581 of 588 outputs exact, all on one culture-history question) came from three comparator LLMs (Sec. 3.1-3.2, Table 1).

On the frozen 100-task REFLEX-Sim benchmark, act-when-confident with LLM fallback reached 0.95 vs 0.88 success with 72.7% fewer strong calls (McNemar p=0.039) and all 66 autonomous tasks succeeded; but Kimi failed the non-inferiority bound and on tau2-style tasks REFLEX had 0.850 vs 0.900 (strong-only) and 0.917 for a cheaper Flash self-escalation cascade, differences unresolved (Sec. 5.1, 5.4-5.6, Tables 1, 3-5).

Single-call error-detection AUROC 0.875/0.745/0.827 vs GPT-6 0.894/0.907/0.831 on RewardBench/JudgeBench/HaluEval; Brier 0.113/0.297/0.196 vs 0.115/0.095/0.213, with Jev's HaluEval advantage reversed on adjudicated labels; temperature scaling fitted on pilot data helped one task and hurt two (Sec. 7.2).

Frozen two-order cascade (Jev then GPT-6) was +0.93 points vs GPT-6 alone at 41% of its fee on 1,610 held-out pairs (JudgeBench -0.74 [-2.22, 0.74]) and matched GPT-6 exactly in a pre-specified live test at 75.5% of its fee; but thresholds had to be chosen on about 100 local labels per workload and routing weakened on style-adversarial pairs (AUROC 0.76 vs 0.84) and reference-free prose (Abstract, Sec. 7.4, 8-9).

On 510 reconstructed InjecAgent cases the original injection selected the attacker target in 9/510 (1.8%) and the enhanced attack in 0%; 24 queries of score-feedback optimisation raised validated ASR only to 3.5% [0.0, 10.0] (18 cases) with confident-hijack rate 0.2%, although attacker probability rose (+0.043 to 0.084) and successes clustered on small-margin cases (Sec. 5.1-5.5, Table 2).

A generic zero-shot question reached median AUROC 0.886 [0.821, 0.952] over 31 alignment-failure benchmarks, beating TF-IDF/length baselines on 25 of 31 and matching the GPT-4o-mini scorer against human labels (kappa 0.809 vs 0.811); but the recommended use needs a threshold fitted on ten labels (median F1 0.706 at 0.5 vs 0.822 cross-validated, gain mostly on unvalidated labels) and parity fails per generator (GPT-3.5 kappa 0.668 vs 0.790) (Sec. 4.1, 4.4, 4.5).

Probabilities calibrated when pooled (ECE 0.047) but not within benchmarks: median per-benchmark ECE 0.168 vs 0.074 expected under perfect calibration, 24 of 31 exceeding the null, from base-rate mismatch (median 0.125); confidence still supports selective use (top-half accuracy 0.793 to 0.933) (Sec. 4.4).

A probability-guided search (<=64 accepted queries) for fluent context additions redirected Jev on 312 of 508 initially correct decisions (61.4%, Wilson 57.1-65.5), 229 ending with >=0.7 on the wrong option; a plain Qwen scorer flipped 64.9% and open typed models (OpenSourceJev, Von) up to 73.2% of their own correct items (Abstract, Sec. 4.2, Table 1).

On runtime-declared templates that change only the question, fine-tuned open Laya returned its trained answer for 0.982-0.995 of item-seed pairs (0.801 act-and-wrong), whereas hosted Jev read the new questions (>=0.98 accuracy on 6 of 8 templates; 0.677 on renamed keys) (Sec. VI-C, Table V).

Jev's gate acted wrongly on at most 0.143 of changed questions (preregistered outcome 6 safe / 1 within bound / 0 violating) vs 0.801 for fine-tuned Laya, but certifying action on any new decision type at alpha=0.05 requires >=19 labels, Jev is 11-29x slower than local models, and labels are simulator-derived (Abstract, Sec. VI-C, IX).

Across 72,000 questions on TREC, CLINC150 and MASSIVE, directly asked category probabilities disagreed with summed fine-label probabilities by mean total variation 0.219-0.349 for Jev and 0.424-0.689 for Laya, which the author calls substantial incoherence (Abstract, Sec. 5, 9).

Decomposing decisions through the label hierarchy changed results: marginalised reconstruction lowered Jev's accuracy by 11.8-22.9 points (CLINC150 91.0% to 68.1%, [-24.9, -20.9]) and raised the much weaker Laya's by 5.6-21.3, so composed decision chains do not reproduce direct decisions (Table 4, Sec. 7).

On MetaMedQA Jev was better calibrated than GPT-6 Sol (ECE 0.063 vs 0.146) but its confidence discriminated worse on DiagnosisArena (AUROC 0.645 vs 0.768); it chose 'I don't know' for 17/162 (10.5%) unanswerable items vs 8.6% for GPT-6 Sol, and was over-confident on every benchmark by 5.8-13.6 points (Sec. 3.3-3.4).

Selective prediction was worse than GPT-6 Sol on two of three benchmarks (AURC 0.087 vs 0.070 on MetaMedQA, 0.303 vs 0.080 on DiagnosisArena; 0.109 vs 0.126 on PubMedQA): 93.4% accuracy at confidence >=0.9 but GPT-6 Sol as accurate at matched coverage, and the authors conclude better calibration gave no selective-prediction advantage (Abstract, Sec. 3.3).

On a 50-way CWE classification of 1,916 CyberSecEval snippets Jev beat all six open-weight LLMs but had lower top-1 than GPT-5.6-Sol (0.458 vs 0.495) with higher top-3/top-5 and similar MRR; diagnosis-guided repair raised the security pass rate 0.635 to 0.707 (LLM-guided 0.661) but broke 89 secure samples (LLM-guided 79) (Abstract, Sec. IV).

Jev's source-attribution x argument interactions were small (US CODEPINK-College Republicans -0.0197; five European pairs |I|<=0.0314, all below the adopted 0.05 reference) vs -0.154 to -0.449 for chat models; the author cautions that Jev used a different rubric with mid-scale scores (1.80-2.43 of 4) and that this does not establish debiasing (Sec. 4, 4.4, App. B).

For evaluating public-policy arguments Jev showed small source effects but compressed, unexplained scores (no written assessment), which the author says reduces the visibility of any bias and limits comparison with chat evaluators; the study does not test deployment at scale (Sec. 4.4, 5, App. B).

On 365 synthetic items with known P(A), Jev's Noul (mean OVL 0.918) and Score (0.886) probabilities tracked ground truth but binary Choice was distorted (0.764; open SemIf 0.629) and less invariant across renderings; an in-sample fitted uncertainty map raised median Choice OVL 0.771 to 0.903 (Table 1, Sec. 3-5, App. A).

On 1,000 exact-posterior worlds Jev failed the operational coherence criterion (all nine relation pass-rate bounds <0.95) and had the largest calibration gap (0.1952) and canonical decision loss (0.1336 vs always-defer 0.10), yet smaller complement, coarsening and permutation residuals than Kev and the generative readouts (e.g. complement 0.0929 vs 0.1155-0.8000) (Sec. 6.1-6.3, Tables 2-3).

Asking the same event through Jev's Event (yes/no) and Choice interfaces gave different act/defer actions on 32.8% of pairs at defer cost 0.10 (post-trained generative readout 34.2%, Kev 14.9%), and inter-interface disagreement certified only 11-52% of error (Abstract, Sec. 6.3, 7, Table 3).

Rotating answer options left accuracy unchanged (MMLU calculation subjects 94.3%), but accuracy fell from 97.2% in English to 37.4% for Nigerian Fulfulde on Belebele and to 33.8-70.3% for 16 African languages on AfriXNLI (English 90.5%); both open LLM references degrade likewise (Sec. 4.5-4.6, Table 6).

Choice probabilities well calibrated (pooled ECE 0.028 over 279,925 answers, unweighted mean 0.061; Qwen 0.063, Gemma 0.208), but multi-label Noul over-predicts yes (mean 0.209 vs observed 0.041) and binary probabilities need task thresholds (UNFAIR-ToS micro-F 0.499 to 0.748) (Sec. 4.3).

Jev put 38.8% of ANLI predictions and 51.3% of its errors on Neutral despite balanced labels; across 36 ordinal datasets decisions used only 67-76% of gold effective support (nominal 87-102%), two random option orders agreed on 74.4% of ordinal items, and finer scales cut utilisation to 26-75% at K=14 (Abstract, Sec. 4.1-4.3).

Decision-level compression on ordinal scales coexists with candidate probabilities that remain broad for most models, so graded probabilities partly preserve scale information that argmax decisions lose (Jev relative utilisation 95.9% at K=2 to 54.5% at K=14) (Sec. 4.3, Conclusion).

Against one due-diligence application, all nine attacker x difficulty combinations broke Jev at least once and the strongest of three adaptive attackers succeeded in 25 of 27 runs (about turn 4, about $0.50 per break); marking content untrusted made no difference (16/27 vs 16/27); Jev 59% overall vs 67-100% for non-reasoning comparators and 19-70% with reasoning enabled (blog tables).

Re-running 5 of 44 Just Ask Jev legs (1,155 items) reproduced AUROC (median absolute difference 0.0036; TensorTrust-hijack 0.9476), but F1 at threshold 0.5 was low (0.158 on TensorTrust-hijack, recall 8.8%) vs 0.947 with a threshold fitted on labels; median F1 gain +0.254 and none of five fitted thresholds was 0.5 (README tables).

In an item-paired XNLI 2x2 the state-language effect on AUROC was +0.3150 [+0.2427, +0.3884] under Chinese criteria and +0.1660 under English for small open typed models (NanoJev, von), and Laya kept a language gap (English AUC 0.984 vs Chinese 0.568) (paper-zh Sec. 4.9, 4.13).

Open small typed models gave uninformative confidence: NanoJev p_true lay entirely in 0.664-0.896 with none below 0.5 and von entirely below 0.474, with heavily overlapping positive/negative ranges (paper-zh Sec. 4.1, 5.2).
Renaming the no-action option to 'witness: observe without acting' (with a short preface) raised its probability by up to 0.28 in otherwise identical situations (Abstract, J2).

Preregistered (48,300 calls): confidence predicted own errors beyond page difficulty (AUROC +0.039 and +0.005, p=.0005) but tracked presentation (over-confident 0.10 on clean pages, under-confident 0.04 on reworked pages at matched accuracy, diff -0.136 [-0.173, -0.099]); with no evidence and no opt-out it answered at 0.82 confidence at chance; with an explicit no-action option it held 0.98 when nothing was left but its action threshold (0.39-0.44) ignored stakes (ideal 0.50-0.90) (Abstract, J1-J2).

On the author's 10 civic triage scenarios Jev reached 100% routing accuracy and schema compliance at 197.6 ms mean and $0.05 per 100,000 queries, while generative LLMs took 3,340-12,682 ms in emergency scenarios and Qwen reached 33.3% standalone accuracy; very small self-built scenario set (Public-service paper Abstract, Table 1, Sec. 5.1-5.2).

Answers were stable across ten runs (spread <=0.08) but rewording the same dilemma moved them much more: trolley diversion 0.99 as a Choice vs 0.78 as a yes/no question, and opposite conclusions on meaning vs survival between framings (paper Sec. IV-F; README).

Round-one answers based on a single word of biography sat as far from 0.5 as better-informed ones, although one extra fact moved answers by a median 0.15 (up to 0.67) and changed three of ten bunker places, so the model did not signal insufficient information (paper Sec. IV; README).

410 requests cost $0.0081 at a median 275 ms whether or not the model was undecided (274 vs 272 ms; humans 4.6-6.8 s), so the difficulty-correlated latency institutions use to flag hard cases disappears; agreement with the film's decisions was partial (11 of 29) (paper Abstract, Sec. IV-A, V).

On the UAV benchmark with ground-truth epistemic uncertainty, open Laya-421M zero-shot reached accuracy 0.399 (majority 0.366), Brier 0.751 and confidence-vs-error AUROC 0.655, collapsing toward the prior while posting an ECE that looks acceptable; ECE varied 0.034-0.113 across option rotations (Abstract, Sec. 5 F6-F7, Conclusion).

A conformal escalation gate built on Laya's confidence returned risk 0.585 at nominal alpha=0.05; a frozen-encoder refit-head control attributes about 70% of the failure to representation (Abstract, Sec. 4.2).

In 26,796 calls on Taiwan's sovereignty Jev's status index (0.40/0.26/0.40 in Traditional/Simplified Chinese/English) was below every generative model and it chose PRC formulations in Simplified Chinese forced choice regardless of option order, yet it never chose a label listing Taiwan under China (Claude Sonnet 5: 42% in Simplified Chinese); rankings depend on the instrument (Abstract, Sec. 4.2-4.6).

Jev was the fastest and cheapest model, but its political defaults in structured outputs depended on instrument, script and stated asker (with a Beijing asker it chose PRC formulations on all three sovereignty questions in Simplified Chinese and English, as did both Claude models); the label-side swap was specific to Claude Sonnet 5 per the addendum (Abstract, Sec. 4.7, 4.9, App. C).

Theory: Lemma 1 proves marginal calibration is not preserved under latent regime shift and every permutation-invariant audit statistic (ECE included) has zero power to detect it; checked only by simulation, 'nothing here is an empirical claim about' Jev (Abstract, Sec. 3, 7).
Theory: Lemma 2 shows thresholding typed scores makes a composed pipeline's action discontinuous, so per-hop calibration audits miss chain-level flips; simulations only (Abstract, Sec. 4, 7).

Hosted Jev flipped 2.9%/1.9% of decisions under option reordering (customer service/voice) and 1.7% between Simplified and Traditional script, whereas open Laya multilingual flipped 20.6%/10.8% and 12.8%, and a Qwen3.5-2B logit probe 2.9%/8.0% and 2.2% (README results table, current version beyond v0.2).

Jev's shipped calibration held on Chinese voice routing (ECE 0.035, n=323; refit did not help) and scam detection (0.952, ECE 0.073, n=21), but open Laya's binary over-confidence exceeded its shipped correction range; the Qwen logit probe collapsed on binary judgments (scam ECE 0.39-0.42) (README key findings 2 and 5; results table).
